newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asia grain/oilseed buyers await new price falls.
newsitem.headline: SE Asia grain/oilseed buyers await new price falls.

text.p: Recent sharp falls in Chicago grains and oilseeds futures have driven Southeast Asian buyers to the sidelines this week on expectations that prices will dive further, regional traders said on Thursday.
"A cloud of bearishness has settled over the market and chased the buyers away," a U.S. trader said. "It's a buyers' market. Nobody is stepping out to be a hero."

"These guys have seen a big drop in prices. If you put yourself in a buyer's shoes, there's no incentive to buy. Why buy today when it seems like it's going lower," another trader in a U.S. trading house added.

Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) December corn futures slid 4-1/4 U.S. cents a bushel to end Wednesday's session at US$2.70-1/4 a bushel. Buyers feel the price may drop to $2.65 a bushel or lower, Singapore-based dealers said.
CBOT November soybean futures slid nine U.S. cents to finish yesterday at $6.89-1/2 a bushel. Corn and soybean futures have fallen more than $1 a bushel since July.
Most buyers are holding back on the belief that the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop report, due by mid-November, will indicate large U.S. corn and soybean crops this year.
"Everybody around here is convinced the corn will be around 9.4 billion bushels and soybeans will be over 2.4 billion bushels," one U.S. dealer said.
"They'll (the buyers) probably sit it out that far. There's certainly a bearish feel to the market," another said.
The USDA's October crop report estimated the 1996 U.S. corn crop would reach 9.012 billion bushels and that soybeans will hit 2.346 billion bushels.
Another factor discouraging buyers is that most have ample cover until the year-end and will not rush pell-mell into the market, traders said.
"Forward cover can wait a while," a dealer said.
A trader in a European commodity house said Indonesia would need about 50,000 tonnes of corn for February/March.
"But the Indonesians can afford to sit it out. There's no rush for them to buy since they just harvested their local crop," one trader said.
Malaysian buyers, who were earlier seeking at least two Handy-sized cargoes of soymeal, have also dropped out of sight, another trader said.
"They've chickened out because they feel prices will come down some more," one dealer said.
Thai buyers are well-stocked and will simply wait for the implementation of a cabinet order slashing tariff rates on imported grains and oilseeds before taking a look at the market.
"Business is really slow. The only game in town recently was the corn tender in the Philippines," one trader said.
He was refering to the 150,000 tonnes of corn awarded by the government's National Food Authority on Tuesday at an average price of $161.10 a tonne C&F.
"They got it reasonably cheap and slightly below the market price," one trader said.
The price of U.S. corn in Southeast Asia eased slightly to around $147-$150 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment on board a Panamax vessel compared with around $148-$150 a tonne C&F last week.
Traders said U.S. soybeans in the region were also down in a range between $295-$296 a tonne C&F from $297-$298 a tonne C&F.
Indian-origin soymeal rose slightly on nearby tightness to be indicated in a wide range between $297-$306 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment against $290-$295 last week.
Quotes for U.S.-origin meal in Southeast Asia dipped to around $282-$283 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment on board a Panamax vessel against $285-$287 a tonne C&F last week, the traders said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
